title: After 15 Years in the Market, AI Didn't Make Me Rich. It Made Me Less Stupid.
author: Cry528
selftext:
I've been investing and trading for over 15 years. I've lived through the aftermath of the financial crisis, multiple bull markets, the COVID crash, the AI boom, and more market panics than I can count. Today I'm financially independent and no longer rely on trading income to pay my bills.

What's funny is that the biggest change in my investing career wasn't finding a better stock, a better indicator, or a better market. It was accepting that my emotions were often the weakest part of my entire system.

When I was younger, I thought experience would eliminate emotional mistakes. I assumed that after enough years, I would stop feeling fear during crashes and greed during rallies. That never happened. Even after a decade in the markets, I still found myself hesitating before entries, taking profits too early, holding losers too long, and convincing myself that "this time is different." The market doesn't care how long you've been trading. It only cares how consistently you execute.

About five years ago I started building simple quantitative models for my personal portfolio. Nothing fancy. Mostly trend-following systems, volatility filters, position-sizing rules, and automated rebalancing. At first I treated them as tools. Over time they became decision-makers. Eventually I realized something uncomfortable: many of my models were outperforming the decisions I made manually. Not because the models were smarter than me, but because they didn't suffer from fear, ego, revenge trading, or FOMO.

When AI tools became more accessible, I started experimenting with them as research assistants rather than prediction machines. I used AI to scan earnings transcripts, summarize news flows, identify unusual sentiment shifts, and help generate hypotheses worth testing. What surprised me most was not the predictive power. It was the efficiency. Tasks that previously took several hours could often be completed in minutes. That gave me more time to focus on risk management and system design, which in my opinion are far more important than trying to predict tomorrow's price movement.

One lesson that took me years to learn is that most traders spend too much time optimizing entries and not enough time optimizing behavior. Everyone wants a signal that predicts the next move. Very few people want to build a system that prevents them from destroying their own account during emotional periods. My best-performing automated strategies aren't the ones with the highest returns. They're the ones that survive bad environments without forcing me to interfere.

That said, I think a lot of people in the AI trading space are making the same mistake traders made with indicators twenty years ago. They're treating AI like a magic solution. Every cycle has a new holy grail. First it was technical indicators. Then social sentiment. Then alternative data. Now it's AI. The technology changes, but human nature doesn't. Most systems eventually fail when market conditions change. The traders who survive are usually the ones who adapt risk rather than chase certainty.

Today roughly 70% of my portfolio decisions are governed by predefined rules and automated processes. The remaining 30% is discretionary. Ironically, the less control I try to exert over every market move, the better my long-term results have become. My biggest edge is no longer finding opportunities. It's avoiding unnecessary mistakes.
